polar-bear.relatives: Polar bears are closely related to brown bears, including grizzlies, and are thought to have evolved from brown bear ancestors living in the Arctic within the last few hundred thousand to around a million years, a short time in evolutionary terms. The two species can still interbreed, and wild hybrids, sometimes called 'pizzly' or 'grolar' bears, have been found in the Canadian Arctic as grizzlies move north. Genetic studies show that brown bears on Alaska's ABC Islands carry polar bear DNA from past interbreeding. Bears as a family, Ursidae, include eight living species, from the sun bear to the giant panda, and are related to seals, sea lions and dogs. Polar bears are the most carnivorous bears, adapted to a diet of fat-rich seals.

narwhal.relatives: The narwhal's only close relative is the beluga, the white whale, and together they form the family Monodontidae. Belugas and narwhals share the Arctic, have no dorsal fin, and occasionally interbreed; a skull of a likely hybrid was found in Greenland in the 1990s. These whales are toothed whales, like dolphins, porpoises and sperm whales, which hunt using echolocation. Fossils suggest that narwhal and beluga relatives once lived in warmer waters, such as the extinct Bohaskaia from Virginia and Denebola from Mexico, and that the family moved into the Arctic more recently. The spiral tusk is unique to the narwhal, and its evolution, from a normal tooth to a tusk that pierces the lip, still raises questions.

blue-whale.relatives: The blue whale is a rorqual, a group of baleen whales with throat pleats that includes the fin whale, sei whale, humpback whale and minke whales. The fin whale, the second-largest animal on Earth, is closely related, and blue and fin whales can interbreed. Several subspecies of blue whale are recognised, including the Antarctic blue whale, the largest, and the smaller pygmy blue whale of the Indian Ocean and South Pacific. Whales evolved from land mammals related to hippos around 50 million years ago, and baleen whales gradually replaced teeth with baleen. Large body size evolved quite recently, within the last few million years, perhaps as krill became more concentrated in seasonal hotspots, making huge size an advantage for filter feeding.

common-octopus.relatives: The common octopus is a cephalopod, a group of molluscs that includes squid, cuttlefish and the nautilus. Cephalopods are relatives of snails and clams, though they lost or internalised their shells; the nautilus still has an external, chambered shell. There are around 300 octopus species, from the tiny star-sucker pygmy octopus to the giant Pacific octopus, which can have an arm span of several metres. Scientists have recently realised that what was called the common octopus may include several closely related species around the world, and the name Octopus vulgaris is now often used only for populations in the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. Octopuses evolved their large brains independently of vertebrates, making them a remarkable example of intelligence arising in a completely separate branch of life.

leatherback-sea-turtle.relatives: The leatherback is the only living member of its family, Dermochelyidae, and it is very different from the six other sea turtle species, such as green, loggerhead and hawksbill turtles, all of which have hard shells. Its lineage split from the other sea turtles over 100 million years ago. Fossil relatives in the same broad group include Archelon, the largest turtle ever known, which lived around 80 million years ago and was about 4.5 metres long. Sea turtles descended from turtles that lived on land, and they still breathe air and lay eggs on land, which ties them to beaches. Their reliance on beaches means that sea-level rise and coastal development are growing threats.

whale-shark.relatives: The whale shark is the only species in its family, Rhincodontidae. It belongs to the carpet sharks, an order that includes nurse sharks, zebra sharks and wobbegongs, which mostly live on the seafloor; the whale shark is the only one that lives in open water. Two other sharks are filter feeders: the basking shark, the second-largest fish, and the deep-sea megamouth shark, discovered only in 1976. Each evolved filter feeding separately. Sharks have existed for more than 400 million years, longer than trees, and their skeletons are made of cartilage, not bone. The famous extinct giant shark megalodon, which reached perhaps 15 to 20 metres, was a predator, unlike the gentle whale shark.

strawberry-poison-frog.relatives: The strawberry poison frog belongs to the poison dart frogs, family Dendrobatidae, a group of around 200 species found in Central and South America. Not all are brightly coloured or toxic; many are brown and harmless. The most toxic, the golden poison frog of Colombia, carries enough toxin to kill several people. The strawberry poison frog's genus, Oophaga, means 'egg-eater', referring to the tadpoles' diet of unfertilised eggs, a habit shared by its closest relatives, such as the harlequin poison frog. Bright warning colours and the ability to store toxins from food evolved several times within the family. Its many colour forms in Bocas del Toro arose as islands were cut off by rising sea levels several thousand years ago.

brown-throated-sloth.relatives: There are six living species of sloth in two groups: the three-toed sloths, including the brown-throated, pale-throated, maned and pygmy three-toed sloth, and the two-toed sloths. The two groups are not as close as they look; they evolved tree-hanging habits separately from different ground-living ancestors. Sloths are related to anteaters and, more distantly, armadillos, together forming a group of mammals that evolved in South America. Their ancestors include giant ground sloths such as Megatherium, which was as big as an elephant and could stand on its hind legs, and lived until about 10,000 years ago. Ground sloths reached North America too, and their bones have been found in Yukon caves. The pygmy three-toed sloth lives only on a single island off Panama and is critically endangered.

jaguar.relatives: The jaguar is the only living Panthera species in the Americas, and its closest relatives are the leopard and the lion. Its ancestors crossed from Asia into North America over the Bering land bridge around 1.5 million years ago. During the ice ages, jaguars were larger and lived as far north as the central United States, and the American lion, a relative of today's lion, also roamed North America. Jaguars survived the extinctions at the end of the last ice age that wiped out many large mammals. Although they look like leopards, jaguars are stockier, with a larger head and shorter tail. Black jaguars are not a separate species; they carry a gene that produces extra dark pigment, as do black leopards, which are often called black panthers.

andean-condor.relatives: The Andean condor is one of the New World vultures, family Cathartidae, along with the California condor, the king vulture and the turkey vulture. Despite their similar lifestyle, New World vultures are not closely related to Old World vultures of Africa, Europe and Asia, which belong to the hawk and eagle family; their bald heads and soaring flight evolved separately. The California condor, the only other condor, came close to extinction in the 1980s, when the last 27 wild birds were captured for breeding; today several hundred fly again. Condor relatives were once much larger: Argentavis, which lived in Argentina about 6 million years ago, had a wingspan estimated at around 6 metres, making it one of the largest flying birds ever.
